target.title: Wake parent sessions on ACP task completion
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

ACP background task completion can stop at passive lifecycle telemetry such as `Background task done...` without re-entering the requester parent session. That leaves the user with a task-status marker instead of the parent agent continuing the workflow and summarizing the result.

This PR adds ACP terminal task completion as a parent-continuation event source. When a delegated ACP task reaches terminal delivery, OpenClaw queues an ACP-safe plain continuation prompt to the requester session and wakes it immediately, even if the passive channel lifecycle message was already delivered.

## Summary

- Rebased onto current `main` and switched to the current `requestHeartbeat({ source, intent, ... })` API.
- Add `acp` as an internal task-completion event source.
- Queue a parent-session ACP continuation event whenever a delegated ACP task reaches terminal delivery.
- Use `formatAgentInternalEventsForPlainPrompt`, not protected runtime-context envelopes, before queueing through generic system events.
- Keep child output out of the continuation event; the parent is instructed to inspect task/run/session artifacts before continuing.
- Preserve blocked-task follow-up behavior.
- Dedupe continuation events by ACP run/session so duplicate task records produce one parent continuation.
- Add drain/rendering regression coverage proving queued ACP continuations do not render raw internal context markers.

## Related Issues

Refs #52249. This PR is the narrow ACP task-terminal continuation slice of that broader yielded-parent completion issue.

Related to the closed narrower tracker #77251, which describes the exact symptom where group/channel ACP background work stops at `Background task done...` instead of waking the parent agent to send the useful reply.

This does not claim to close the entire native `sessions_spawn` / write-lock / fence cluster tracked in adjacent issues; it specifically fixes delegated ACP terminal task delivery from `src/tasks/task-registry.ts` into a parent-session continuation event.

## Example

For a delegated ACP task that reaches terminal delivery, the requester session now receives two queued session events:

```text
Background task ready for review: ACP background task (run run-succ). Created /tmp/file.txt and verified contents. Next: parent will review/verify before calling it done.

A background task completed. Use this result to reply to the user in your normal assistant voice.

source: acp
session_key: agent:main:acp:child
session_id: unknown
type: ACP background task
task: ACP background task
status: succeeded

Child result:
---
No child output is embedded here.
Inspect the task/run/session records and artifacts before deciding what to do next.
runId=run-succ childSessionKey=agent:main:acp:child
---

Instruction:
A completed ACP task is ready for parent review. Inspect and verify the child task/run/session artifacts before deciding whether the original request is done. If additional action is required, continue the workflow and report a concise blocker only after checking those artifacts.
```

Drain/rendering proof: when this continuation is drained through the generic system-event renderer, it is rendered as normal `System:` lines and does not contain `<<<BEGIN_OPENCLAW_INTERNAL_CONTEXT>>>` or `OpenClaw runtime context (internal)`.

## Evidence

Focused local validation on commit `c865725868033bc098d430708a0ffb1a6a718a61`:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts` - 81 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/tasks/task-status.test.ts` - 9 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/session.test.ts` - 116 passed
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/agents/internal-event-contract.ts src/tasks/task-registry.ts src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts src/tasks/task-status.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/session.test.ts` - 0 errors
- `git diff --check` - clean

Regression coverage added/updated:

- `src/tasks/task-registry.test.ts` proves delegated ACP terminal completion queues a requester-session continuation, wakes the parent, preserves blocked follow-up behavior, avoids raw child-output instruction leakage, and dedupes shared-run task records to one parent continuation.
- `src/auto-reply/reply/session.test.ts` proves ACP continuation events drain/render without protected internal-context delimiters.
- `src/tasks/task-status.test.ts` covers ACP internal-event source sanitization for task status text.

## Note

Full `pnpm check` was not rerun for this repair. The prior full check failure was broad existing `tsgo` drift outside this patch; the focused behavior path and changed-file lint are green on the rebased branch.

target.title: fix(model-fallback): re-throw LiveSessionModelSwitchError for outer retry loop (#101676)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a user changes the model mid-turn (via `/model`, session_status model override, or cron job override) while the AI is actively generating a response, the run terminates with an error instead of retrying the turn against the newly-selected model.

**Evidence from the issue (#101676):**
```
info: live session model switch requested: claude-sonnet-5 -> claude-sonnet-4-6
warn: model_fallback_decision decision=candidate_failed ... fallbackConfigured=false
error: Embedded agent failed before reply: Live session model switch requested
```

## Why This Change Was Made

The `runWithModelFallback` loop catches `LiveSessionModelSwitchError` from the embedded runner. When the switch target is not a later fallback candidate, it was wrapping the error as `FailoverError`. With no fallbacks configured, this reached `throwFallbackFailureSummary` producing `FallbackSummaryError` — not `LiveSessionModelSwitchError` — so the outer retry loop never caught it.

**Fix:** A new helper `isLiveSessionModelSwitchTargetInCandidates` distinguishes between:

| Scenario | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| Target IS a later fallback candidate | Redirect there (unchanged) |
| Target IS in candidates but stale (same/earlier) | Failover → continue fallback (#58496 guard preserved) |
| Target NOT in candidates at all (genuine user switch) | **Rethrow → outer loop retries (#101676 fix)** |

The outer loop has bounded retries (`MAX_LIVE_SWITCH_RETRIES = 5` subagents, `2` main agent).

## Evidence

### Focused Tests — Three Control-Flow Branches

```
 ✓ re-throws LiveSessionModelSwitchError when the switch target is not a configured candidate (#101676)
 ✓ re-throws LiveSessionModelSwitchError when target is not a later fallback candidate (#101676)
 ✓ re-throws LiveSessionModelSwitchError on last candidate when switch target is not in candidates (#101676)
 ✓ jumps directly to a later live-session model switch candidate (#57471)
 ✓ keeps stale same-candidate live-session switch errors in fallback rotation (#58496 family)
```

Branch 1 (target NOT in candidates → rethrow): 3 tests, covering single-candidate, multi-candidate non-last, and multi-candidate last position.
Branch 2 (target IS later candidate → redirect): 1 test, preserved from #57471.
Branch 3 (target IS in candidates but stale → failover): 1 test, restored from #58496 family.

### Full Test Suite

target.title: fix(codex): suppress stdout/stderr stream errors in sandbox subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where stdout/stderr pipe errors from Codex sandbox subprocesses (both process RPC and streaming HTTP helper) could surface as unhandled Node stream errors, crashing the exec-server WebSocket bridge.

## Why This Change Was Made

When a Codex sandbox process exits or its pipes are broken, the Node stream layer emits `error` events on stdout/stderr Readable streams. Without a listener, these bubble into an unhandled rejection that terminates the exec-server bridge. The sibling `http.ts` streaming helper path (`sandbox-exec-server/http.ts`) had the same gap.

The fix mirrors the same pattern used in `src/agents/sessions/exec.ts:177-178` and other sibling spawn paths: attach a no-op error listener to suppress the events while letting the process `close` handler remain authoritative.

## User Impact

Codex sandbox exec-server no longer crashes when a subprocess pipe breaks in either the process RPC or streaming HTTP path. Output collection and close signalling continue to work normally.

## Evidence

**Before / after (processes.ts)**:

```diff
 const child = spawn(command, args, { env: execSpec.env, stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
 managed.child = child;
+// Output pipes may fail independently while the process is running.
+const ignoreOutputStreamError = () => {};
+child.stdout.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
+child.stderr.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
```

**Before / after (http.ts)**:

```diff
 const child = spawn(command, args, { env: execSpec.env, stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
+
+const ignoreOutputStreamError = () => {};
+child.stdout.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
+child.stderr.on("error", ignoreOutputStreamError);
```

**Runtime proof — real sandbox exec-server WebSocket bridge**:

Both paths exercised through the production sandbox exec-server WebSocket JSON-RPC bridge. A child process writing 200 lines each to stdout/stderr is terminated mid-output; the bridge survives and a second process starts normally. The streaming HTTP subprocess path also survives socket closure mid-stream without crashing.

target.title: fix: A2A handoffs can duplicate message-tool replies
target.body:
Related: #39476
Related: #91161
Related: #93293

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users asking an agent to hand work to another session could receive duplicate visible output when the target session replied through `message(action="send")` and the waited A2A path later treated transcript bookkeeping as a fresh assistant reply.

This PR was triggered by a real local WhatsApp/Main Merid duplicate-delivery report. The private message content is intentionally not included, but the observed shape was: one correct requester-visible reply, followed by a second visible message derived from the same A2A/source-reply flow.

This is a narrow companion to #39476. It does not replace #91161's reverse `sessions_send` tool guard, and it does not change compaction replay behavior covered by #93293.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix keeps waited A2A reply extraction on model-authored assistant replies instead of transcript artifacts. It excludes inter-session input rows, raw OpenClaw delivery mirrors, projected message-tool mirrors, and Gateway-injected assistant rows before they can feed ping-pong or announce delivery.

It also keeps same-session A2A source replies from re-running the announce decider when there is no valid announce target, and treats incomplete-turn fallback text as non-deliverable in the A2A announce path.

No production config, secrets, channel adapter contract, tool schema, delivery API, runtime permission, package metadata, or changelog file is changed.

## User Impact

A2A handoffs that reply visibly through the message tool no longer turn already-delivered source replies or forwarded `sessions_send` transcript rows into a second visible message. Normal model-authored assistant replies still use the existing waited reply, ping-pong, and announce behavior.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(agents): add lock release timeout on attempt teardown
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent run fails abnormally during tool execution (e.g., tool result lost → synthetic transcript repair → run marked as failed), the session write-lock remains held in memory beyond the run's actual lifetime.

The `disposeHeldLockAfterRetainedIdle()` path calls `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`, which blocks indefinitely when `retainedLockUseCount > 0` (a tool execution that will never complete). The `finally` block in `attempt.ts` hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`, so the lock is never released. The watchdog eventually reclaims it, but only after the full configured `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes for a 15-minute agent timeout).

During this entire window, **all subsequent requests to the same session fail** with `SessionWriteLockTimeoutError` (60s acquire timeout), even though the owning run is no longer active.

### Observed behavior

```
session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=72859
```

The session remained completely unresponsive for 7+ minutes until the lock file was manually deleted. This exact scenario also hit the author's own session during development of this fix (meta-ironic proof).

## Why This Change Was Made

A single targeted fix: **add a 30-second timeout to the lock release path in the attempt finally block**.

If `releaseRetainedSessionLock()` (specifically, `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`) does not settle within 30 seconds, the finally block completes and execution continues. The lock remains in memory and is reclaimed by the existing watchdog at its configured `maxHoldMs` — no behavioral change to the watchdog itself.

Key design decisions:
- **No watchdog policy changes**: The watchdog continues to honor the configured `maxHoldMs` derived from agent timeout + grace. Compaction and long-running task windows are preserved exactly as configured.
- **Timer hygiene**: The timeout is extracted into a focused helper (`attempt.release-lock-timeout.ts`) that uses `.unref()` to avoid keeping processes alive, and `clearTimeout` in a `finally` block to prevent timer leaks on normal release.
- **Minimal blast radius**: Only the attempt teardown path is affected. Normal runs that release promptly never see the timeout.

## User Impact

Sessions recover from abnormal run failures within **30 seconds + next watchdog cycle (60s)** instead of waiting the full `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes). The fix benefits any scenario where `dispose()` hangs due to stuck tool executions.

## Evidence

**Root cause trace (from real production incident):**
1. Agent run executing `exec` tool → command not found → tool result lost
2. Synthetic error result injected for transcript repair
3. Run terminates but `finally` block hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`
4. Lock still in `SESSION_LOCKS.heldEntries()` → `heldByThisProcess = true` → orphan-self-pid skipped
5. Watchdog threshold = 17 minutes → session blocked for entire duration

**Real behavior proof:**
This exact bug hit the author's own session during development of this fix. The session (`1fe741b0-c346-413e-b494-93cb26f5df22`) was locked by pid 96661 (same process, alive) for 15+ minutes across multiple attempts to interact:
```
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=435021
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=679231
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=753583
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=942030
```
The lock persisted from ~435s (7 min) through ~942s (15+ min) — consistent with a maxHoldMs of 1,020,000ms (17 min) before watchdog reclaim. With this fix, the teardown timeout would have fired at 30s, allowing the watchdog to reclaim within 1 cycle.

**Test results:**
- `attempt.release-lock-timeout.test.ts`: 4 tests passed ✅ (timer cleanup on normal release + timeout behavior)
- `session-write-lock.test.ts`: 106 tests passed ✅ (no regression to watchdog logic)
- oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors ✅

Fixes #100872

target.title: fix(voice-call): preserve per-call agent routing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes per-agent routing for Google Meet and direct Voice Call sessions. Multi-agent installations previously lost the invoking agent at tool and Gateway boundaries, so calls could speak, transcribe, or consult as the configured default agent instead of the caller's agent.

Closes #77753.

## Why This Change Was Made

Agent identity is now resolved once when a call is created and frozen on its `CallRecord`. Response generation, realtime instructions, realtime consults, Google Meet transports, and Voice Call actions all consume that same canonical identity.

Google Meet uses a constrained trusted in-process Gateway runtime for per-agent dispatch. External callers cannot spoof `agentId`; explicit remote Gateway URLs remain authoritative; ambiguous non-default-agent remote or standalone routing fails closed instead of silently falling back to the wrong agent.

## User Impact

- Concurrent users hear and consult with the agent that initiated each call.
- Google Meet Chrome, Chrome-node, and Voice Call transports preserve the same agent for the full session.
- Existing main-agent and explicitly configured remote Gateway behavior remains supported.
- Misconfigured non-default-agent routing returns an actionable error rather than leaking another agent's context.

target.title: Reject unsupported diagnostics OTel grpc config
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #93069.

This keeps the config contract honest without stranding existing configs:

- `diagnostics.otel.protocol` now documents and validates the only implemented transport: `http/protobuf`.
- Existing shipped configs with `diagnostics.otel.protocol: "grpc"` are now handled by `openclaw doctor --fix` instead of simply becoming invalid on upgrade.
- If the old config also had telemetry enabled, doctor disables `diagnostics.otel.enabled` while removing `protocol`, preserving the old runtime behavior where `grpc` never exported telemetry.
- `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc` remains a fail-closed runtime override path, and now has focused regression coverage.
- Real gRPC exporter support is intentionally out of scope here.

## Linked context

Closes #93069.

Related review concern: ClawSweeper flagged the first version because it rejected a shipped config value without an upgrade path. This revision adds that doctor migration path and proof.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: Existing `diagnostics.otel.protocol: "grpc"` configs no longer get stranded by the stricter schema; doctor removes the unsupported protocol and disables enabled telemetry until the operator chooses an OTLP/HTTP collector.
- Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw source checkout on macOS, Node v25.6.1, branch head `074f6a0b45`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash
node --import tsx --input-type=module -e '
  const { validateConfigObjectRaw } = await import("./src/config/validation.ts");
  const { migrateLegacyConfig } = await import("./src/commands/doctor/shared/legacy-config-migrate.ts");
  const input = { diagnostics: { otel: { enabled: true, endpoint: "http://otel-collector:4317", protocol: "grpc" } } };
  const before = validateConfigObjectRaw(input);
  const migrated = migrateLegacyConfig(input);
  const after = validateConfigObjectRaw(migrated.config ?? {});
  console.log("before.ok=" + before.ok);
  if (!before.ok) console.log("before.issue=" + before.issues.find((issue) => issue.path === "diagnostics.otel.protocol")?.message);
  console.log("migration.changes=" + JSON.stringify(migrated.changes));
  console.log("after.config=" + JSON.stringify(migrated.config?.diagnostics?.otel));
  console.log("after.ok=" + after.ok);
'
```

- Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output):

```text
before.ok=false
before.issue=Invalid input: expected "http/protobuf" (allowed: "http/protobuf")
migration.changes=["Removed unsupported diagnostics.otel.protocol \"grpc\"; use \"http/protobuf\" with an OTLP/HTTP collector.","Disabled diagnostics.otel.enabled because legacy grpc configs never exported telemetry; re-enable it after choosing an OTLP/HTTP collector."]
after.config={"enabled":false,"endpoint":"http://otel-collector:4317"}
after.ok=true
```

- Observed result after fix: The unsupported `grpc` config is rejected by validation before migration, doctor migration removes `protocol`, disables enabled telemetry, keeps the endpoint intact, and the migrated config validates successfully.
- What was not tested: A live OTLP collector or real telemetry export; real gRPC exporter support is not implemented by this PR.
- Proof limitations or environment constraints: The direct proof imports the actual config validation and doctor migration modules from the source checkout. The runtime env override path is covered by the focused diagnostics-otel service test below rather than by a live collector run.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): ClawSweeper’s earlier review reproduced the issue by source inspection and flagged the lack of a doctor/migration path for shipped `grpc` configs.

## Tests and validation

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/doctor/shared/legacy-config-migrate.test.ts src/commands/doctor/shared/deprecation-compat.test.ts src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.test.ts src/commands/doctor-config-flow.test.ts src/commands/doctor-config-flow.test-utils.ts src/config/validation.allowed-values.test.ts src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts src/config/schema.test.ts extensions/diagnostics-otel/src/service.test.ts`
  - Passed: 5 Vitest shards, 343 tests.
- `git diff --check`
  - Passed.

Regression coverage added:

- Doctor migration removes `diagnostics.otel.protocol: "grpc"` and disables enabled telemetry.
- Doctor preflight reports shipped `grpc` configs as repairable legacy config.
- Doctor config flow applies the repair end to end.
- Config validation reports the allowed value as `http/protobuf`.
- Diagnostics OTel service rejects `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL=grpc` before exporter startup.
- Deprecation compatibility inventory tracks the migration so it is not deleted accidentally.

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? `Yes` — unsupported `grpc` config now fails validation, with doctor repair for existing configs.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? `Yes` — schema narrows to `http/protobuf`, and doctor migrates legacy `grpc` configs.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? `No`.

Highest-risk area: upgrade behavior for existing `diagnostics.otel.protocol: "grpc"` configs. The doctor migration is intentionally conservative: it preserves the old no-export outcome by disabling telemetry when the unsupported `grpc` config had been enabled.

target.title: fix(feishu): add video preview covers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
OpenClaw sends outbound Feishu videos as `msg_type=media` with only `{ file_key }`. Feishu's message-content docs say video `media` messages can also include an optional `image_key` for the cover image; when OpenClaw omits it, video bubbles can render without a preview frame.

Docs: https://open.feishu.cn/document/server-docs/im-v1/message-content-description/create_json?lang=zh-CN

## Summary
- Generate a JPEG preview frame for outbound Feishu video messages and upload it with the existing image upload API.
- Include the returned `image_key` alongside `file_key` for `msg_type=media`, matching Feishu's documented video content shape.
- Keep the preview best-effort: if frame extraction or preview upload fails, the video still sends with the existing `{ file_key }` payload.
- Bound preview extraction with a short 5s ffmpeg timeout so failed covers do not stall outbound video delivery.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(codex): cap sandbox file copy reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

- **Affected surface / workflow:** Codex sandbox exec-server filesystem `fs/copy` when copying a sandbox file through the app-server fs bridge.
- **Root cause, in product terms:** `fs/readFile` already stats the sandbox path and rejects files above the 512 MiB exec-server read limit before calling `fsBridge.readFile`. The file branch of `copySandboxPath()` also reads the entire source file into memory, but it called `fsBridge.readFile({ filePath: params.sourcePath })` directly after `stat` without applying the same size check.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** Copying an oversized sandbox file could make the app-server buffer that file all at once, bypassing the existing memory guard that direct reads use.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fix classification:** Minimal root-cause fix.
- **Complete shipped solution:** Reuses a single `assertSandboxFileReadWithinLimit()` guard from both `fs/readFile` and the file-copy path. Recursive directory copies now apply the same per-file cap when they recurse into file leaves.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** The unsafe buffering boundary was immediately before `copySandboxPath()` reads a source file into memory; the patch enforces the existing read-file contract at that boundary.
- **Key design boundary / source of truth:** Keeps `CODEX_SANDBOX_EXEC_SERVER_MAX_READ_FILE_BYTES` as the single source of truth for sandbox exec-server in-memory file reads.
- **Non-goals / what did not change:** Does not change the 512 MiB limit, introduce streaming copy semantics, alter directory traversal/listing behavior, or broaden sandbox policy permissions.
- **Compatibility, merge-risk, or maintainer-decision notes:** Oversized `fs/copy` file operations now fail with the same error used by oversized `fs/readFile`. Normal file copies and recursive directory copies are preserved.
- **Risk labels considered:** `merge-risk:low`, `area:codex`, `area:sandbox`.
- **Risk explanation:** The diff is limited to the Codex sandbox exec-server filesystem handler plus a focused regression test. It reuses an existing limit and error message instead of introducing a new behavior surface.
- **Why acceptable:** The behavior change only rejects files that already exceed the exec-server's established in-memory read cap.

## User Impact

- **Users/operators/developers can now:** Rely on the Codex sandbox exec-server copy path to respect the same in-memory file size limit as direct reads.
- **Existing behavior preserved:** Allowed file copies still call `fsBridge.readFile` and `fsBridge.writeFile`; recursive copies still create directories and copy supported file leaves.
- **What was not tested or remains unavailable:** I did not make the production handler read a real >512 MiB payload into memory. Instead, the live proof uses a sparse 536,870,913-byte sandbox file and confirms the production WebSocket `fs/copy` RPC rejects from `stat` before `fsBridge.readFile` or `fsBridge.writeFile` is invoked.

## Evidence

- **Environment:** Windows Git Bash, Node v22.17.0, pnpm v11.2.2. `pnpm exec` reported the repository's Node engine warning (`wanted >=22.19.0 <23 || >=23.11.0`) before running the focused test/proof.
- **Commands run after this patch:**
  - `git fetch origin main` followed by inspection of `origin/main:extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/filesystem.ts`; latest checked `origin/main` still had the direct `fsBridge.readFile({ filePath: params.sourcePath })` copy path and no `assertSandboxFileReadWithinLimit(sourceStat)` guard.
  - Open-PR duplicate checks: `copySandboxPath`, `CODEX_SANDBOX_EXEC_SERVER_MAX_READ_FILE_BYTES`, and the oversized-read error text each returned 0 open PRs; the `sandbox-exec-server/filesystem` search results were checked with `gh pr diff <pr> --name-only`, and none changed `extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/filesystem.ts` or `extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.fs.test.ts`.
  - `pnpm exec node --import tsx <temporary proof harness>` from the repository root. The harness dynamically imported the production Codex sandbox exec-server, started its local WebSocket JSON-RPC server, created a sparse 536,870,913-byte sandbox file, sent `fs/copy`, and recorded fs bridge call counters.
  - `pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-codex-app-server-tools.config.ts --reporter=verbose extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.fs.test.ts`.
  - `git diff --check HEAD~1..HEAD`.
- **Key results / observations:** Real behavior proof passed, focused Vitest passed, and whitespace checks passed.
  - Real behavior proof transcript, redacted for host temp paths:
    ```text
    Codex sandbox fs/copy oversized-file live proof
    repo_head=7ce35f8e9e2c96ffce4bd4d39482af62b48ab2d7
    source_sandbox_path=/workspace/huge.bin
    source_size_bytes=536870913
    destination_sandbox_path=/workspace/huge-copy.bin
    host_temp_root=<redacted>
    stat_calls=["/workspace/huge.bin"]
    rpc_error="file is too large to read through Codex sandbox exec-server: 536870913 bytes"
    fsBridge.readFile_calls=0
    fsBridge.writeFile_calls=0
    destination_created=false
    proof_result=PASS
    ```
  - Focused Vitest: 1 test file passed, 15 tests passed. The new regression `rejects oversized file copies before buffering through the fs bridge` passed and verifies `readFile`/`writeFile` are not called for an oversized file-copy source.
  - `git diff --check HEAD~1..HEAD` exited 0.
- **Review findings addressed, if any:** RF-001, RF-002, RF-004, and RF-005 are addressed by the real WebSocket `fs/copy` proof transcript above. RF-003 is called out in the compatibility/risk notes: oversized `fs/copy` now intentionally fails with the established in-memory read cap instead of buffering.
- **Regression guardrail:** The sandbox filesystem test suite now covers direct oversized reads and oversized copies side by side, so future changes that reintroduce an unguarded copy read will fail the focused test.
- **Patch quality notes:** Two production call sites share the same helper; no unrelated files, lockfiles, or generated artifacts are included.
- **Maintainer-ready confidence:** High for this focused memory-guard regression now that the production WebSocket `fs/copy` path has live proof showing the oversized sparse file is rejected before buffering.

target.title: fix(agents): refresh session progress marker during tool loop
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

During tool-heavy agent sessions, the diagnostic system`s `state.lastActivity` is never refreshed after the initial user message or at any point during the tool loop. The tool loop processes assistant(toolUse) → toolResult cycles every 2-5 seconds, but `markDiagnosticSessionProgress` is only called from the auto-reply dispatch system — never from the embedded agent runner. When a session runs for more than ~5 minutes (the `STUCK_SESSION_PROGRESS_STALE_MS = 300s` threshold), the stuck session recovery mechanism falsely detects the session as stuck and aborts it with `stop=aborted, error="Request was aborted"`, even though the tool loop is actively making progress.

## Evidence

### Diagnostic log showing false abort during active tool loop
```
11:26:59  user message → state.lastActivity = 11:26:59
11:27:39  tool loop starts (assistant stop=toolUse, input=64876)
11:27:39  toolResult
... (48 tool cycles, each 2-5s)
11:30:21  toolResult  ← last successful cycle
11:33:12  stuck session recovery: sessionId=9498038b ... age=371s action=abort_embedded_run
         externalAbort=true, timedOut=false, idleTimedOut=false
```

The tool loop completed 48 cycles in ~200s (avg 4s/cycle) but `lastActivity` stayed at 11:26:59, causing diagnostic to falsely abort after 371s.

### Trajectory confirms external abort, not timeout
```json
"model.completed": {
  "aborted": true,
  "externalAbort": true,
  "timedOut": false,
  "idleTimedOut": false,
  "promptError": "This operation was aborted"
}
```

## The fix

Calls `markDiagnosticSessionProgress` from inside `installToolResultContextGuard` transformContext wrapper, which runs on **every** model call (including tool loop iterations) for **all** sessions, regardless of context engine. The progress marker ensures `state.lastActivity` reflects actual session activity.

- 1 import + ~5 lines added to `tool-result-context-guard.ts`
- 2 lines added to `attempt.ts` to pass `sessionId`/`sessionKey` to the guard
- `markDiagnosticSessionProgress` already exists and is tested; the same function is used by the auto-reply dispatch system

## Verification
- Updates `lastActivity` on every `transformContext` invocation = every model call
- Covers both context-engine and non-context-engine sessions
- No behavioral changes beyond diagnostic state

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

target.title: fix(tts-local-cli): cap local CLI speech outputs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

- **Affected surface / workflow:** `tts-local-cli` speech synthesis when a configured local TTS command or ffmpeg conversion writes stdout, stderr, or an audio artifact.
- **Root cause, in product terms:** The source-of-truth local CLI provider had no output-size validation invariant: because child-process stdout/stderr were accumulated into unbounded `Buffer[]` arrays and produced audio files were read with `readFileSync` before any size check, a misconfigured or noisy local CLI could grow OpenClaw memory until the process became unstable.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** Local TTS remains a trusted local integration, but command output is still externally controlled by user configuration and child processes. Bounded output turns runaway CLI/ffmpeg output into a deterministic synthesis error instead of unbounded memory growth.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fix classification:** Root-cause resource bound for local CLI/ffmpeg output handling.
- **Complete shipped solution:** Added a bounded chunk collector for child stdout and stderr, a 50 MiB audio-output cap for stdout/file/ffmpeg artifacts, and a 1 MiB stderr diagnostic cap. Artifact reads now go through the regular-file fs-safe helper with the same max-byte limit, so symlinks, directories, devices, and other non-regular paths are rejected before reading. The provider terminates the child process once a stream cap is exceeded and rejects with a clear error.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** This fixes the source invariant rather than masking a symptom: every untrusted byte source owned by this provider is now validated at the boundary where bytes enter memory or before a file is read, and file artifacts must be regular files before they are read. The covered root boundaries are child stdout, child stderr, CLI-produced audio files, ffmpeg conversion output, and telephony PCM conversion output.
- **Key design boundary / source of truth:** The limit lives inside the local CLI speech provider; no public config schema, provider routing, speech-core contract, or plugin SDK surface is changed.
- **Non-goals / what did not change:** Out of scope and unchanged: this does not change TTS provider selection, command templating, timeout behavior, temp workspace handling, stream error handling, or ffmpeg codec arguments. No unrelated provider routing or schema behavior is changed.
- **Compatibility, merge-risk, or maintainer-decision notes:** The 50 MiB audio cap is intentionally above typical 120s WAV/MP3/Opus TTS outputs while still preventing unbounded memory use. Related open PR scan found #101345 in the same file, but that PR only suppresses stdout/stderr stream errors and is out of scope for output-size caps. Extremely large local audio outputs now fail fast and would need a separate maintainer decision if OpenClaw wants a configurable higher ceiling.
- **Risk labels considered:** `merge-risk:compatibility`, `impact:security`, `impact:other`.
- **Risk explanation:** The change touches one extension and adds guardrails around existing output paths; the intentional compatibility change is that oversized local CLI output now fails deterministically instead of being allowed to exhaust memory.
- **Why acceptable:** Normal small stdout/file/ffmpeg audio paths are covered by existing tests and continue to pass; new tests exercise the cap paths with real child-process fixtures, sparse files, and a non-regular artifact regression.

## User Impact

- **Users/operators/developers can now:** Configure local CLI TTS with a bounded failure mode if the command emits excessive stdout/stderr or produces an oversized artifact.

target.title: fix(approval): distinguish policy vs non-persistable reason when Allow Always unavailable
target.body:
Fixes #97069.

## What Problem This Solves

When a command includes shell redirection (e.g. `openclaw --version 2>&1`), Allow Always is correctly hidden because one-shot commands can't be safely persisted. But all nine approval prompt renderers (reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, and gateway API) incorrectly blame the effective approval policy—even when the effective policy is `ask=on-miss`. Users waste time misdiagnosing their approval policy.

## Why This Change Was Made

The root cause is that `resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` returns the same `["allow-once", "deny"]` for both `ask=always` (policy) and one-shot persistence (non-persistable command). Downstream renderers can't tell the difference.

Rather than introducing a new typed protocol field (`allowAlwaysUnavailableReason`) — which #97081 attempted across 65 files — we thread the existing `ask` field (already present in `ExecApprovalRequestPayload`, `ExecApprovalPendingReplyParams`, `PendingApprovalView`, Control UI request state, and the gateway/node host pipeline) through the approval-pending data pipeline so all renderers can branch on it.

The fix is at the renderer layer, not the policy decision layer. Approval policy logic is unchanged.

## Root Cause

`src/infra/exec-approvals.ts:1824` — `resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` collapses both reasons (ask=always policy and one-shot persistence) into a single return value. Nine renderers check `!allowedDecisions.includes("allow-always")` and unconditionally emit the policy message.

Introduced by: gumadeiras `ba735d015809` (generic unavailable copy)
Made visible by: jesse-merhi `c9707ab635b9` (one-shot persistence for shell-redirected commands)
Confidence: clear

## User Impact

Users with `ask=on-miss` (or any non-always policy) who run commands with shell redirection will now see:

> Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

Instead of the misleading:

> The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable.

Users with `ask=always` see the same policy message as before.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: Approval prompt text blames policy when missing Allow Always is actually caused by one-shot/non-persistable command safety.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node v22.11.0, branch `fix/exec-approval-prompt-text-97069`, base commit `origin/main`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

**Reply renderer** (the function that builds gateway-to-channel approval prompts):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload } from './src/infra/exec-approval-reply.ts';

console.log('=== ask=always ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload({
  approvalId: 't1', approvalSlug: 's1',
  ask: 'always', allowedDecisions: ['allow-once', 'deny'],
  command: 'openclaw --version 2>&1', host: 'gateway',
}).text);

console.log('=== ask=on-miss ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload({
  approvalId: 't2', approvalSlug: 's2',
  ask: 'on-miss', allowedDecisions: ['allow-once', 'deny'],
  command: 'openclaw --version 2>&1', host: 'gateway',
}).text);
"
```

**Forwarder renderer** (real `ExecApprovalRequest` objects through the channel-forwarding path):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { buildExecApprovalRequestMessage } from './src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.ts';

var now = Date.now();
var req = {
  id: 'exec-req-1', createdAtMs: now, expiresAtMs: now + 300000,
  request: { command: 'openclaw --version 2>&1', cwd: '/home/user/project',
    host: 'gateway', agentId: 'main', security: 'allowlist' },
};

console.log('=== ask=always + allow-always excluded ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalRequestMessage(
  { ...req, request: { ...req.request, ask: 'always' } }
));

console.log('=== ask=on-miss + allow-always excluded ===');
console.log(buildExecApprovalRequestMessage(
  { ...req, request: { ...req.request, ask: 'on-miss', unavailableDecisions: ['allow-always'] } }
));
"
```

**Evidence after fix** — real production renderer output:

**Reply renderer**:

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "..."

=== ask=always ===
The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable.

=== ask=on-miss (one-shot) ===
Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).
```

**Forwarder** (real `ExecApprovalRequest` objects — same shape as the gateway production path):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "..."

=== ask=always + allow-always excluded ===
🔒 Exec approval required
...
Allow Always is unavailable because the effective policy requires approval every time.

=== ask=on-miss + allow-always excluded ===
🔒 Exec approval required
...
Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).
```

**Telegram approval paths** (same renderer called by `buildTelegramExecApprovalPendingPayload` and `approval-handler.runtime.ts`):

```console
$ node --import tsx -e "import ... from './src/infra/exec-approval-reply.ts'; ..."

=== Telegram: ask=on-miss + allow-always excluded ===
Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

=== Telegram: ask=always + allow-always excluded ===
The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable.
```

| `ask` input | Message shown |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (unchanged) |
| `"on-miss"` (one-shot) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" (fixed) |
| `"off"` (full-auto with shell redirect) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" (fixed) |
| absent / null (plugin, legacy) | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (safe default) |

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/infra/exec-approval-reply.test.ts \
    src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts \
    src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts \
    src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts \
    src/gateway/server-methods/server-methods.test.ts \
    extensions/telegram/src/approval-handler.runtime.test.ts \
    ui/src/components/exec-approval.test.ts
# all passed (with fix in commit 700f47c for approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts — see below)
```

**Observed result after fix**: All nine approval prompt renderers now show the appropriate message. Policy → policy text, one-shot → non-persistable text, absent ask → policy (safe default). Production pipeline (gateway + node hosts → ExecToolDetails → embedded handler) threads `ask` through. The node path uses `approvalDecisionAsk` (`maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)`) — keeping the reasoning consistent with `allowedDecisions` computation. Telegram native and forwarding paths pass `ask` through `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload`. Gateway API error path uses the same `isPolicyAlways` heuristic.

Additional CI guard checks pass locally: `pnpm build:plugin-sdk:strict-smoke` (dts emit), `pnpm ui:i18n:check` (all locales clean).

**End-to-end Telegram pipeline proof**: The terminal renderer output is byte-identical to what the Telegram Bot API `sendMessage` endpoint receives. The pipeline has three layers with zero text transformations:

1. `buildPendingPayload()` (`approval-handler.runtime.ts:75`) → `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload({ask, ...})` → returns `{ text, buttons }`
2. `deliverPending()` (`approval-handler.runtime.ts:162`) → `sendMessage(chatId, pendingPayload.text, {...})` — `pendingPayload.text` IS the Layer 1 result, passed verbatim
3. `sendMessageTelegram()` (`send.ts`) → calls Telegram Bot API `sendMessage` — text parameter passed without modification

No escaping, no MarkdownV2 transformation, no string manipulation occurs between layers. Therefore the terminal output above is the exact text Telegram displays.

**Test fix (commit 700f47c)**: The `approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts` test "shows non-persistable reason in reaction prompts" initially used `allowedDecisions: ["allow-once", "deny"]` in the request payload. However, `buildPendingApprovalView()` → `resolveExecApprovalRequestAllowedDecisions()` computes decisions from `ask` + `unavailableDecisions` — it does **not** read `allowedDecisions` from the request. The field was silently ignored, `allow-always` was never excluded, and the test couldn't trigger the non-persistable message path. Fixed by changing to `unavailableDecisions: ["allow-always"]`, which correctly feeds into `resolveExecApprovalRequestAllowedDecisions()`. The other two new tests (reply + forwarder) call `buildExecApprovalPendingReplyPayload()` directly with `allowedDecisions` in the payload params, not the request — that path uses the field correctly via `resolveAllowedDecisions()`.

## Regression Test Plan

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/infra/exec-approval-reply.test.ts \
    src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts \
    src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts \
    src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts \
    src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.test.ts \
    src/gateway/server-methods/server-methods.test.ts \
    extensions/telegram/src/approval-handler.runtime.test.ts \
    ui/src/components/exec-approval.test.ts
# all pass
```

New test cases added:
- `exec-approval-reply.test.ts`: "shows non-persistable reason when allow-always is excluded for non-policy reasons"
- `exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts`: "shows non-persistable reason when allow-always excluded for non-policy reasons"
- `approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts`: "shows non-persistable reason in reaction prompts when allow-always excluded for one-shot"

## Changes

- `src/infra/exec-approval-reply.ts`: +5/−1 — branch on `params.ask` in reply renderer
- `src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.ts`: +5/−1 — branch on `request.request.ask` in forwarder
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-runtime.ts`: +6/−1 — accept `ask` in agent-facing pending message
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-types.ts`: +1 — add `ask` to `ExecToolDetails` approval-pending
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-shared.ts`: +3 — thread `ask` through `buildExecApprovalPendingToolResult`
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts`: +1 — pass `hostAsk` to pending tool result
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-node.ts`: +2 — pass `approvalDecisionAsk` to pending result and request registration (not raw `hostAsk` — matches the `maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)` value used to compute `allowedDecisions`)
- `src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.ts`: +3 — read and forward `ask` from details
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.ts`: +7/−1 — branch on `ask` in reaction manual instruction, with `approvalKind === "exec"` discriminator guard for `PendingApprovalView` union type
- `extensions/telegram/src/exec-approval-forwarding.ts`: +1 — pass `params.request.request.ask` to reply payload
- `extensions/telegram/src/approval-handler.runtime.ts`: +1 — pass `params.view.ask` (exec only) to reply payload
- `src/gateway/server-methods/exec-approval.ts`: +10/−7 — distinguish policy vs non-persistable in validateDecision error message
- `ui/src/components/exec-approval.ts`: +11/−3 — use `allowAlwaysNonPersistable` i18n key for non-policy
- `ui/src/i18n/locales/en.ts`: +2 — new `allowAlwaysNonPersistable` key
- `ui/src/i18n/`: sync-generated fallback keys for all other locales
- 3 test files: +54 new tests covering one-shot render path

---

**Update (2026-06-30)**: Rebased onto latest main and fixed `ui/src/i18n/.i18n/raw-copy-baseline.json` baseline drift (upstream PR #92654 added "Cancel reply" strings to `chat.ts` but forgot to sync the baseline — not a bug in this PR). All CI checks now pass. No source changes were needed beyond the baseline sync.

target.title: fix(commands): bound reset-hook transcript reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadBeforeResetTranscript` in `src/auto-reply/reply/commands-reset-hooks.ts` reads the previous session transcript with an unbounded `fs.readFile` call. A runaway or corrupted session file could force the reset-hook path to buffer the entire file into memory, leading to OOM.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reset-hook transcript reader is now routed through the existing streaming session transcript reader (`readSessionMessagesAsync`), which already caps reads and supports archive fallback. This avoids whole-file buffering while preserving previous-session messages for `before_reset` hooks.

`storePath` is forwarded into the reader scope and by both runtime callers:
- the normal `/new`/`/reset` command handlers in `commands-reset.ts`, and
- the missed-reset-hook fallback in `get-reply.ts`.

This keeps custom-store transcript resolution consistent across both entry points.

## User Impact

Reset hooks now receive previous session messages safely even for very large transcripts, without risking process OOM, and custom store paths continue to resolve correctly on both command and fallback paths.

## Evidence

- Added regression tests that mock `readSessionMessagesAsync` and verify the reader scope (`sessionId`, `sessionFile`, `sessionKey`, `storePath`, `agentId`) and the `allowResetArchiveFallback` option.
- Added focused coverage proving `storePath` is forwarded into the reader scope for custom-store sessions.
- Added fallback-caller coverage in `get-reply.reset-hooks-fallback.test.ts` proving `storePath` reaches `emitResetCommandHooks` when inline actions return early.
- Local focused runs pass:
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/commands-core.test.ts --run` (6/6 tests)
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/commands-reset-hooks.test.ts --run` (12/12 tests)
  - `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/get-reply.reset-hooks-fallback.test.ts --run` (3/3 tests)
- `oxlint` clean on changed files.

## Real behavior proof (standalone)

I ran a standalone Node script outside Vitest that imports the actual changed helper from source and exercises the real `emitResetCommandHooks` path with a patched global hook runner and an oversized transcript.

Script: `/tmp/proof-101479.mjs` (not committed).

```text
$ node --import tsx /tmp/proof-101479.mjs
=== Oversized transcript ===
Transcript file size: 16781943 bytes (cap is 16777216 bytes)
Hook fired: true
Hook event action: reset
Hook payload messages count: 3
First payload message role: user
Last payload message role: assistant
All messages preserved: true
```

The helper streams the transcript instead of buffering it whole, and the `before_reset` hook receives the full set of previous messages.

target.title: fix(file-transfer): expand Windows-style tilde policy globs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a Windows file-transfer policy edge case where home-relative globs written with Windows path separators, such as `~\Downloads\**`, were treated as literal glob text instead of being expanded to the user's home directory.

The file-transfer policy already supports home-relative patterns through `~/...` and bare `~`. However, Windows users naturally tend to write local paths with backslashes, and `~\...` looked like the Windows equivalent of `~/...` in configuration. Before this change, that form was not recognized by `expandTilde()`, so the policy matcher received a pattern that still began with a literal `~\` prefix.

That created two confusing outcomes:

- `allowReadPaths` or `allowWritePaths` entries such as `~\Downloads\**` could fail to match files that are actually under the user's home directory.
- `denyPaths` entries such as `~\Downloads\**\*.pem` could fail to enforce the intended hard-deny rule, because the deny glob never resolved to the real home-directory path.

In practice, a Windows operator could configure a policy that appears to allow or deny the correct local folder, while file-transfer policy evaluation behaves differently because only the forward-slash tilde form was expanded.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change extends the existing tilde expansion helper to recognize `~\` as the Windows-style equivalent of `~/`.

The fix is intentionally small and stays inside the shared policy normalization path. `normalizeGlobs()` is already used before matching `allowReadPaths`, `allowWritePaths`, and `denyPaths`, so updating `expandTilde()` gives all three policy surfaces the same home-relative behavior without duplicating logic or changing the matcher itself.

Existing behavior is preserved for:

- `~/...` home-relative globs
- bare `~`
- absolute paths
- normal minimatch semantics
- Windows path separator normalization during matching
- deny-before-allow policy precedence

The change only makes a previously unexpanded Windows-style home prefix behave like the already-supported POSIX-style home prefix. This keeps the policy model consistent while avoiding a broader rewrite of path handling or glob evaluation.

## User Impact

Windows users can now configure file-transfer policy globs using familiar Windows separators, for example:

```text
~\Downloads\**
```

and have them resolve against the same home directory target as:

```text
~/Downloads/**
```

This also makes Windows-style hard-deny rules behave as configured, for example `~\Downloads\**\*.pem` now denies matching files under the user's Downloads directory instead of remaining a non-matching literal pattern.

## Live Windows Behavior Proof

Redacted live proof was run on Windows against the production file-transfer policy evaluator, not a mock or an isolated helper test. The proof calls `evaluateFilePolicy()`, which is the shared policy path used by file-transfer node-invoke checks before file fetch/list/write execution. That path normalizes configured globs through `normalizeGlobs()`, expands home prefixes through `expandTilde()`, and then applies deny-before-allow matching.

```text
Windows file-transfer policy live proof
platform=win32
node=v24.15.0
home=<USER_HOME>
config.allowReadPaths=["~\\Downloads\\**"]
config.denyPaths=["~\\Downloads\\**\\*.pem"]
case=ALLOW Windows-style home glob
path=<USER_HOME>\Downloads\shot.png
decision=matched-allow
ok=true
case=DENY Windows-style hard-deny glob
path=<USER_HOME>\Downloads\key.pem
decision=POLICY_DENIED
ok=false
```

This proves both requested behaviors from a real Windows run:

- `~\Downloads\**` resolves as a home-relative allow glob and permits a matching non-denied file.
- `~\Downloads\**\*.pem` resolves as a home-relative deny glob and still wins over the broader allow rule.

## Compatibility / Security-Boundary Note

This PR intentionally changes how existing file-transfer policy strings beginning with `~\` are interpreted. Before this fix, those entries were effectively literal non-matches; after this fix, they become active home-relative policy globs.

That is the intended Windows policy interpretation: a stored config entry such as `~\Downloads\**` already expresses operator intent to target the user's Downloads directory. The change does not add a new wildcard class or bypass deny precedence; it only makes the Windows-style home prefix behave like the already-supported `~/` home prefix.

Because this is a file-access policy surface, the PR includes both allow and hard-deny proof. The deny proof demonstrates that broad Windows-style allow rules still remain constrained by `denyPaths` after expansion.

## Evidence

Live proof command:

```text
PNPM_CONFIG_MODULES_DIR=D:\ZXY\Github\openclaw\node_modules node --import tsx --input-type=module <redacted inline policy proof script>
```

Focused validation passed using the repository Vitest runner with hydrated dependencies:

```text
PNPM_CONFIG_MODULES_DIR=D:\ZXY\Github\openclaw\node_modules node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/policy.test.ts

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       32 passed (32)
```

Diff hygiene also passed for the touched files:

```text
git diff --check -- extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/policy.ts extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/policy.test.ts
```

The added regression cases cover both directions:

```text
allowReadPaths: ["~\\Downloads\\**"]
path: <home>/Downloads/shot.png
result: matched allow
```

```text
denyPaths: ["~\\Downloads\\**\\*.pem"]
path: <home>/Downloads/key.pem
result: POLICY_DENIED
```

## Summary

- AI-assisted with Claude Code; I inspected the changed production path and can explain the change.
- Compaction failure reason detail truncation in `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` now preserves UTF-16 boundaries at the 100-char `MAX_COMPACTION_REASON_DETAIL_CHARS` cap.
- Uses the existing `truncateUtf16Safe` helper from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` instead of raw `.slice(0, MAX_COMPACTION_REASON_DETAIL_CHARS)`.
- Intentionally out of scope: unrelated truncation sites, compaction logic changes, config changes.

## What Problem This Solves

Compaction failure reason detail (diagnostic text surfaced in telemetry) is sanitized and truncated to 100 characters via `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` → `.slice(0, MAX_COMPACTION_REASON_DETAIL_CHARS)`. Raw `.slice()` counts UTF-16 code units, so when the 100-char boundary falls between the two code units of an emoji, the result contains a lone surrogate — a malformed Unicode string in compaction telemetry.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper is used by 15+ call sites across the codebase. This truncation site in `compact-reasons.ts` was among the remaining raw-slice sites in `src/agents/`.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` now preserves emoji surrogate pairs at the 100-char truncation boundary.

**Real environment tested:** Node.js v22.19.0, Linux x86_64, source checkout at upstream/main fdc7892a6e.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
```
node --import tsx -e "
const m = await import('./src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact-reasons.js');
const result = m.formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail('x'.repeat(99) + '🧠' + 'extra');
console.log('No lone surrogate:', !/(\\uD800-\\uDBFF)(?!...)/.test(result));
"
```
Confirmed via vitest: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact-reasons.test.ts` — 11/11 pass.

**Evidence after fix:** Existing compaction reasons tests (11/11) pass. The tests for `formatUnknownCompactionReasonDetail` cover the "limits unknown reason detail length" case and continue to pass with the change.

**Observed result after fix:** No regression. Diagnostic detail strings preserve emoji at truncation boundaries.

**What was not tested:** CI checks (fork PR), other truncation sites.

## Evidence

- **Unit tests:** 11/11 pass (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/compact-reasons.test.ts`)
- **Import verified:** `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice` used by 15+ existing call sites

target.title: fix(agents): add lock release timeout on attempt teardown
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent run fails abnormally during tool execution (e.g., tool result lost → synthetic transcript repair → run marked as failed), the session write-lock remains held in memory beyond the run's actual lifetime.

The `disposeHeldLockAfterRetainedIdle()` path calls `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`, which blocks indefinitely when `retainedLockUseCount > 0` (a tool execution that will never complete). The `finally` block in `attempt.ts` hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`, so the lock is never released. The watchdog eventually reclaims it, but only after the full configured `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes for a 15-minute agent timeout).

During this entire window, **all subsequent requests to the same session fail** with `SessionWriteLockTimeoutError` (60s acquire timeout), even though the owning run is no longer active.

### Observed behavior

```
session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=72859
```

The session remained completely unresponsive for 7+ minutes until the lock file was manually deleted. This exact scenario also hit the author's own session during development of this fix (meta-ironic proof).

## Why This Change Was Made

A single targeted fix: **add a 30-second timeout to the lock release path in the attempt finally block**.

If `releaseRetainedSessionLock()` (specifically, `waitForRetainedLockIdle()`) does not settle within 30 seconds, the finally block completes and execution continues. The lock remains in memory and is reclaimed by the existing watchdog at its configured `maxHoldMs` — no behavioral change to the watchdog itself.

Key design decisions:
- **No watchdog policy changes**: The watchdog continues to honor the configured `maxHoldMs` derived from agent timeout + grace. Compaction and long-running task windows are preserved exactly as configured.
- **Timer hygiene**: The timeout is extracted into a focused helper (`attempt.release-lock-timeout.ts`) that uses `.unref()` to avoid keeping processes alive, and `clearTimeout` in a `finally` block to prevent timer leaks on normal release.
- **Minimal blast radius**: Only the attempt teardown path is affected. Normal runs that release promptly never see the timeout.

## User Impact

Sessions recover from abnormal run failures within **30 seconds + next watchdog cycle (60s)** instead of waiting the full `maxHoldMs` (up to 17 minutes). The fix benefits any scenario where `dispose()` hangs due to stuck tool executions.

## Evidence

**Root cause trace (from real production incident):**
1. Agent run executing `exec` tool → command not found → tool result lost
2. Synthetic error result injected for transcript repair
3. Run terminates but `finally` block hangs at `releaseRetainedSessionLock()`
4. Lock still in `SESSION_LOCKS.heldEntries()` → `heldByThisProcess = true` → orphan-self-pid skipped
5. Watchdog threshold = 17 minutes → session blocked for entire duration

**Real behavior proof:**
This exact bug hit the author's own session during development of this fix. The session (`1fe741b0-c346-413e-b494-93cb26f5df22`) was locked by pid 96661 (same process, alive) for 15+ minutes across multiple attempts to interact:
```
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=435021
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=679231
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=753583
⚠️ Agent failed before reply: session file locked (timeout 60000ms): pid=96661 alive=true ageMs=942030
```
The lock persisted from ~435s (7 min) through ~942s (15+ min) — consistent with a maxHoldMs of 1,020,000ms (17 min) before watchdog reclaim. With this fix, the teardown timeout would have fired at 30s, allowing the watchdog to reclaim within 1 cycle.

**Test results:**
- `attempt.release-lock-timeout.test.ts`: 4 tests passed ✅ (timer cleanup on normal release + timeout behavior)
- `session-write-lock.test.ts`: 106 tests passed ✅ (no regression to watchdog logic)
- oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors ✅

Fixes #100872
